_comment: How to check, by hand, the applicable requirements no automated check can settle and no question in security-notes.json or design-questions.json already asks. One line each, written as an instruction to somebody who is not a programmer: what to go and look at, and what would count as the wrong answer. Nothing here credits anything — the report shows these as still unverified, with the instruction beside them, which is the whole point. A requirement that already has a question in one of the other two catalogs is deliberately absent, and crates/sv-check/tests/human_checks.rs refuses an entry that appears in both.

checks.title: Steps cannot be skipped or done out of order
checks.how: Take a flow with more than one step — checkout, sign-up with a confirmation, anything with a "next" button. Write down the address of the last step. Start the flow again, and go straight to that address without doing the steps before it. It should refuse. Then try the steps in the wrong order, and try the same step twice. Describing the flow in securevibe.toml as `flow` under [stack.run.users] lets `sv report --run` try the first two skips for you; the wrong order and the repeated step are still yours.

checks.title: The certificate on the live site is one browsers trust
checks.how: Open the live site in a browser and click the padlock. It should show a certificate issued by a public authority, with a date that has not passed, and the name should match the address. A warning page, or a certificate the app generated for itself, means no visitor can tell your site from an impostor.

checks.title: Nothing is past the update deadline you set
checks.how: Write the time frames from your security notes into securevibe.toml as `[policy] fix-within-days`, one number of days per severity, then run `sv report --advisories DIR` (or `sv audit`) against a local advisory database. It lists the packages with a known vulnerability and puts the ones past your time frame first. Those are the answer to this one. Without the numbers it counts every known vulnerability as late, whatever its age.

checks.title: The business limits you wrote down are the ones the app enforces
checks.how: Take each limit from your security notes — so many of something per person, so many per day — and try to go past it in the app. Try it slowly and then quickly, and from two accounts at once if the limit is meant to be global.

checks.title: Two people cannot book the same thing
checks.how: Only where something is limited in number: a seat, a slot, the last item in stock. Open the app in two browsers, get both to the moment of booking the same one, and confirm both as close together as you can. Exactly one should succeed.

checks.title: The banned word list is actually used
checks.how: Take a word from the list you wrote down — the app's name, your organization's name — and try to register an account using it as the password, or with it inside a longer password. It should be refused. Listing the words in securevibe.toml under [policy] as `context-words` lets `sv report --run` try the first one for you, through the app's own sign-up.

checks.title: Passwords from known breaches are refused
checks.how: Try to register with a password known to have been breached. `Password123!` and `qwerty123456` will do; haveibeenpwned.com/Passwords lists more. The app should refuse it and say why, without telling the person anything about other accounts. `sv report --run` tries one such password through the app's own sign-up, but one refusal only supports this: it does not show the whole list is checked.

checks.title: Getting in needs more than a password
checks.how: Sign in and note everything you were asked for. A password alone is a single factor. A code from an app or a security key is a second one. If there is only a password, that is the answer to this one; if you have decided a password alone is enough, ASVS asks for the reasoning to be written down.

checks.title: There is no forgotten way in
checks.how: List every way somebody can become signed in: the password form, any "sign in with" button, magic links by email, API keys, an admin back door, an old mobile app. Compare that with the list in your security notes. Anything not on the list is what this asks about, and each way in should be as strong as the others.

checks.title: Losing a second factor does not become the easy way in
checks.how: Only where people sign in with a second factor. Go through losing it as a person would: what does support ask for before restoring access? If the answer is less than what was asked when the account was set up, the recovery path is now the weakest way in.

checks.title: Being away signs you out
checks.how: Sign in, then leave the app alone for longer than the idle timeout you wrote down, without clicking anything. Come back and reload a private page. You should be asked to sign in again.

checks.title: A session does not last forever
checks.how: Sign in and keep using the app past the maximum lifetime you wrote down. Staying active must not keep it alive forever — at the limit you should be asked to sign in again even mid-use.

checks.title: Secrets live in something built to hold them
checks.how: List where each password, key, and token the app needs actually comes from: a key vault or your host's secret store, an environment variable, or a file in the code. Say who can read each one, and how you would replace one if it leaked. A secret nobody can rotate is the answer to this one.

checks.title: Nothing internal is reachable from outside
checks.how: From a browser that is not signed in, and ideally not on your network, try the addresses that exist for you rather than for visitors: /docs, /swagger, /metrics, /health, /debug, /admin, /.git. Each should either refuse or not exist.

checks.title: You know which of your data is sensitive
checks.how: List every kind of information the app stores, including what it writes to logs and what it keeps in backups. Mark each with how much it would matter if it got out. Anything you cannot place is the thing to look at, and remember that encoded is not the same as protected.

checks.title: Nothing sensitive is handed to an outside service
checks.how: Open the app in a browser with the network panel recording, sign in, and use it normally. Look at every request going somewhere that is not your own address — analytics, error reporting, fonts, chat widgets. Check what is in each, including the address of the page, which often carries names or record numbers.

checks.title: Sensitive data is handled the way your notes say
checks.how: Take each protection you wrote down — encrypted, kept for so long, never in logs — and check the app against it. Search the logs for the data that should never appear there, and confirm that something really deletes records when their time is up.

checks.title: Time-consuming features cannot cause a loss of availability
checks.how: Take each time-consuming or resource-demanding feature you documented — an export, a report, an AI request, image processing. Start several at once from one account and see whether the rest of the application stays usable. The defenses you wrote down should stop any one person causing a loss of availability for everybody else.

checks.title: Logs go only where your inventory says
checks.how: Compare the log destinations in your inventory with where they really go: files on the server, your host's logging, any outside service, and anything printed to the console. A destination nobody wrote down is one nobody is watching or protecting.

checks.title: The events you said would be logged really are
checks.how: Do each thing your notes say gets logged — a failed sign-in, a permission refused, a record deleted — then look in the logs and confirm each one is there with enough detail to tell who and when. Then try something that should be refused, such as posting a form with a field the app does not expect, and check that the refusal was logged too.

checks.title: Uploaded files are scanned for viruses
checks.how: Find where a file someone uploads is stored before anyone downloads it, and check whether it is scanned by antivirus software on the way in: your host's upload service may offer this, or a scanner such as ClamAV can be added. Try uploading the harmless EICAR test file, which every antivirus scanner recognizes. If the app accepts it and serves it back, known malicious content would be served too.

checks.title: The app judges how reliable each AI answer is
checks.how: Ask your AI coding tool to show you where the app decides how confident it is in an answer the model generated, before showing it. Look for a score or a check, not just the model's text passed straight through. If the answer is shown whatever the model said, the reliability of generated answers is not being assessed.

checks.title: A doubtful AI answer is blocked or replaced
checks.how: With the confidence check from the item above, find the threshold below which an answer is not shown, and what the app shows instead: a fallback message such as "I'm not sure, please contact us". Try asking the AI something it cannot know about your business. It should fall back rather than invent an answer.

checks.title: The AI model has had safety training
checks.how: Look up which model the app uses (your AI coding tool can tell you where it is named) and open the provider's model card or safety documentation. Check that it describes alignment or safety training against disallowed content. Models from the major providers do; a model you downloaded or trained yourself may not, and then this is yours to arrange.

checks.title: The AI's safety is tested again whenever the model changes
checks.how: Write down a short list of prompts the app must refuse or answer carefully, and keep it in version control beside the code. Each time the model is updated or its version changes, run the list again and compare the answers. Check whether this happens today; if nobody reruns anything when the model changes, the answer is no.

checks.title: The AI has been tried against known attacks
checks.how: Try the well-known attacks on the AI part of your app yourself: ask it to ignore its instructions, to reveal its system prompt, to role-play its way past a rule, or hide an instruction inside a document or image it reads. Write down which ones it resisted. A tool such as garak runs many of these adversarial techniques at once.

checks.title: The AI is hardened against tricky inputs
checks.how: Take the attacks from the item above that worked, and check what the app now does about them: input it filters, instructions it keeps apart from what a visitor types, answers it checks before showing. Try each attack again. Hardened means each one that worked before now fails.

checks.title: Someone copying the AI by asking it everything would be noticed
checks.how: Look at what the app records about the questions people ask the AI: who asked, how many, how fast. Check whether anything watches that record for the pattern of someone systematically asking thousands of varied questions to copy what the model knows, the query pattern of an extraction attempt, and warns somebody.

checks.title: Unusual behavior toward the AI is spotted
checks.how: Check whether the app watches for conversations that look like probing: the same question retried many times with small changes, excessive retry attempts, or one visitor trying many different tricks in a row. Try it yourself and look for whether anything was flagged or anyone told.

checks.title: Jailbreak and prompt-injection attempts are recognized
checks.how: List the rules the app uses to recognize attacks aimed at the AI: jailbreak phrasings, prompt injection hidden in documents it reads, attempts to extract its system prompt. Try a few coordinated attempts from two accounts at once, and check whether the rules catch them and something is recorded.

checks.title: A person reviews the code the AI wrote
checks.how: Look at how changes to the app get in: check that every change your AI coding tool wrote is read and approved by a qualified person before it goes live, and that the reviewer is not the same person who asked the AI for the code. The AI agent does not count as the human reviewer. If changes go straight from the AI to the live app, the answer is no.

checks.title: The AI coding tools themselves are attacked on purpose, on a schedule
checks.how: Check whether anyone regularly tries to trick the AI tools that help build the app: a pull request, issue, or comment with a hidden instruction, a known jailbreak, or a request to add a harmful package. Write down when this was last done and what it found, and whether each finding was tracked until fixed. If it has never been done, schedule the first red-team exercise.
